title: The Sad Story of William James Sidis
summary: Josh and Chuck tell the story of William James Sidis (pronounced SIDE-iss), a child prodigy whose parents, Boris and Sarah Sidis, Russian-Jewish immigrants, tried to educate him from toddlerhood. They cover the parents' progressive child-rearing philosophy, Boris's psychology work and feud with Freud, Billy's early achievements and Harvard admission at age eleven, his 1909 lecture on four-dimensional bodies, the media frenzy and invasion of privacy that followed, the family sanitarium year, his later low-paid accounting work, his book The Animate and the Inanimate, the 1937 New Yorker profile and lawsuit, and his death in 1944 at 46. The episode closes with listener mail about metal gods and A C/D C.

segments.title: Opening banter and introduction to William James Sidis
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open with casual banter about potluck food, then introduce the episode as a cautionary tale about a child prodigy, media sensationalism, and parenting, and discuss pronunciation of the name Sidis.

segments.title: Prodigies, nature versus nurture, and the Sidis parents' backgrounds
segments.summary: The hosts discuss child prodigies in general and Billy's well-rounded giftedness, the nature-versus-nurture question, and the background of his Russian immigrant parents Boris and Sarah, including Boris's jailing in Russia for teaching peasants and their rapid academic success in America.

segments.title: Boris Sidis's psychology career and Sarah's parenting checklist
segments.summary: Boris's views on education (learn fundamentals and reason from them, reject memorization), his psychology career and opposition to Freud, and Sarah's progressive parenting checklist, which the hosts note holds up in places but was undermined by the family's showing off of Billy.

segments.title: Billy's early childhood achievements and the press
segments.summary: The hosts list reported early accomplishments of Billy, including reading and languages at a young age, rapid school progress, and writing books. They note that some anecdotes may be exaggerated. They describe Harvard admission at age nine (entering at eleven) and photographers waiting outside his home.

segments.title: Lack of socialization, Harvard lecture, and IQ estimates
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the lack of play and peer socialization in Billy's upbringing. They describe his 1910-era lecture to the Harvard Mathematical Club on four-dimensional bodies at age eleven, MIT professor Daniel Comstock's praise, retroactive IQ estimates, and Boris's essay Philistine and Genius, which provoked public backlash against the family.

segments.title: Harvard years, celibacy vow, and Rice Institute teaching
segments.summary: Billy's difficult time at Harvard dormitories, his graduation cum laude at sixteen in 1914, his public vow of celibacy and seclusion, and his brief teaching post at Rice Institute, where he was younger than his students.

segments.title: Socialism, arrest, and the family sanitarium
segments.summary: Billy returns to Harvard Law and becomes involved in socialism and libertarian-leaning causes. He is arrested at a May Day rally, where he falls in love with Martha Foley. He is then taken to the family sanitarium in New Hampshire for about a year, and his relationship with his parents deteriorates.

segments.title: Later life, accounting jobs, and The Animate and the Inanimate
segments.summary: After the sanitarium year, Billy takes low-level accounting and adding-machine jobs, moving on when coworkers recognize him, while writing prolifically under pseudonyms. The hosts describe his book The Animate and the Inanimate, which discusses dark matter, black holes, and reverse entropy.

segments.title: New Yorker profile, lawsuits, and death
segments.summary: The New Yorker sent a reporter to befriend Sidis and then published a 1937 profile that he found humiliating. He sued for invasion of privacy and libel; the privacy suit was lost and the magazine settled out of court. Sidis died in 1944 at forty-six of a cerebral hemorrhage, and Time ran the obituary 'Prodigious Failure.'

segments.title: Good Will Hunting connection and Four-dimensional space resource
segments.summary: The hosts mention that Sidis may have partly inspired the film Good Will Hunting, and Josh recommends J. D. Norton's explainer on four-dimensional space.

segments.title: Listener mail: metal gods and A C/D C
segments.summary: Listener Kirk from White Rock BC challenges the claim that Bruce Dickinson is the metal god, citing Rob Halford. Listener Gunner agrees that A C/D C is overrated. The hosts joke about Flash in the Pan.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Closing reminder to contact the show by email and a standard iHeartRadio sign-off.
